title: Closed points of a product
statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be schemes of finite type over a field $K$ and
$z\in X\times_KY$ with images $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$. Then $z$
is a closed point of $X\times_KY$ if and only if $x$ and $y$ are
closed points.

proof.text: Put $P=X\times_KY$. By the definition of finite type, choose finite affine open covers $X=\bigcup_i\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ and $Y=\bigcup_j\operatorname{Spec}B_j$, with each $A_i,B_j$ a finitely generated $K$-algebra. By [lem-weil-pbc-open-fibre-product] their products are open subschemes of $P$, with images $p_1^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}A_i)\cap p_2^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}B_j)$, and these cover $P$: every point has an image in some member of each cover. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] each is $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i\otimes_KB_j)$. If $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ generate $A_i$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_t$ generate $B_j$, then $a_\nu\otimes1$ and $1\otimes b_\mu$ generate the tensor algebra: every pure tensor of polynomials is the product of the two corresponding polynomials in these generators, and every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors. Thus this is a finite affine cover by finitely generated $K$-algebras, so $P$ is of finite type over $K$ by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism].

source.place: Tags 01JR (lemma-open-fibre-product) and 01JQ (lemma-fibre-product-affines); explicit finite-generator argument for finite type

proof.text: If $z$ is closed in $P$, [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a), applicable by step 1, makes $\kappa(z)$ finite-dimensional over $K$. The projections induce $K$-compatible field homomorphisms $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(z)$ and $\kappa(y)\to\kappa(z)$ by [def-weil-residue-field]. Each is injective: its kernel is an ideal in a field and cannot contain $1$. Their images are $K$-vector subspaces of $\kappa(z)$, so have finite dimension. Consequently $\kappa(x)$ and $\kappa(y)$ are finite extensions of $K$, and [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a), now applied to the given finite-type schemes $X,Y$, makes both $x,y$ closed.

source.place: Proof, first sentence: closed z implies finite residue fields and closed images

proof.text: Conversely suppose $x,y$ closed. By [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a), $L=\kappa(x)$ and $M=\kappa(y)$ are finite extensions of $K$. Choose finite $K$-bases $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $L$ and $f_1,\ldots,f_t$ of $M$. The $rt$ elements $e_i\otimes f_j$ span $A=L\otimes_KM$: expand both factors of a pure tensor in these bases and distribute, then use that pure tensors span. Thus $A$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $K$-algebra.

source.place: Proof, converse: tensor product of the two finite residue fields is finite-dimensional

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-point-residue-field], applied to $X\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ and $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}K$, the kernel $\mathfrak p$ of $A\to\kappa(z)$ is prime, and $\kappa(z)$ is isomorphic to the fraction field of $D=A/\mathfrak p$, compatibly with the two residue-field maps and hence with $K$. Here the base residue field is $K$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum].

source.place: Tag 01JT (lemma-points-fibre-product), last sentence of the statement

proof.text: The quotient $D$ is spanned over $K$ by the images of the finite spanning set of $A$ from step 3, and is a nonzero integral domain because $\mathfrak p$ is prime. For $0\ne a\in D$, multiplication by $a$ is an injective $K$-linear endomorphism of this finite-dimensional vector space, so it is surjective; there is $b\in D$ with $ab=1$. Thus $D$ is a field. Its fraction field is therefore $D$ itself, and the isomorphism of step 4 shows that $\kappa(z)$ is finite over $K$.

source.place: Proof, converse: residue field of the finite algebra is finite; elementary quotient and multiplication argument replacing the unnecessary Artinian decomposition

proof.text: Apply [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a) to the finite-type $K$-scheme $P$ from step 1. The finiteness of $\kappa(z)/K$ proved in step 5 gives that $z$ is closed in $P$, completing the reverse implication.

source.place: Proof, final clause: finite residue field implies closed z
